div.head: THE ACHARNIANS
by Aristophanes
div.p: [Translator uncredited. Footnotes have been retained because they provide the meanings of Greek names, terms and ceremonies and explain puns and references otherwise lost in translation. Occasional Greek words in the footnotes have not been included. Footnote numbers, in brackets, start anew at [1] for each piece of dialogue, and each footnote follows immediately the dialogue to which it refers, labeled thus: f[1].

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: This is the first of the series of three Comedies—The Acharnians, Peace and Lysistrata—produced at intervals of years, the sixth, tenth and twenty-first of the Peloponnesian War, and impressing on the Athenian people the miseries and disasters due to it and to the scoundrels who by their selfish and reckless policy had provoked it, the consequent ruin of industry and, above all, agriculture, and the urgency of asking Peace. In date it is the earliest play brought out by the author in his own name and his first work of serious importance. It was acted at the Lenaean Festival, in January, 426 B.C., and gained the first prize, Cratinus being second.

Its diatribes against the War and fierce criticism of the general policy of the War party so enraged Cleon that, as already mentioned, he endeavoured to ruin the author, who in The Knights retorted by a direct and savage personal attack on the leader of the democracy.

The plot is of the simplest. Dicaeopolis, an Athenian citizen, but a native of Acharnae, one of the agricultural demes and one which had especially suffered in the Lacedaemonian invasions, sick and tired of the ill-success and miseries of the War, makes up his mind, if he fails to induce the people to adopt his policy of peace at any price, to conclude a private and particular peace of his own to cover himself, his family, and his estate. The Athenians, momentarily elated by victory and over-persuaded by the demagogues of the day—Cleon and his henchmen, refuse to hear of such a thing as coming to terms. Accordingly Dicaeopolis dispatches an envoy to Sparta on his own account, who comes back presently with a selection of specimen treaties in his pocket. The old man tastes and tries, special terms are arranged, and the play concludes with a riotous and uproarious rustic feast in honour of the blessings of Peace and Plenty.
Incidentally excellent fun is poked at Euripides and his dramatic methods, which supply matter for so much witty badinage in several others of our author's pieces.

Other specially comic incidents are: the scene where the two young daughters of the famished Megarian are sold in the market at Athens as suck[l]ing-pigs—a scene in which the convenient similarity of the Greek words signifying a pig and the pudendum muliebre respectively is utilized in a whole string of ingenious and suggestive double entendres and ludicrous jokes; another where the Informer, or Market-Spy, is packed up in a crate as crockery and carried off home by the Boeotian buyer.
The drama takes its title from the Chorus, composed of old men of Acharnae.

div.stage: SCENE: The Athenian Ecclesia on the Pnyx; afterwards Dicaeopolis' house in the country.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.note: A name invented by Aristophanes and signifying a just citizen.
sp.p: What cares have not gnawed at my heart and how few have been the pleasures in my life! Four, to be exact, while my troubles have been as countless as the grains of sand on the shore! Let me see! of what value to me have been these few pleasures? Ah! I remember that I was delighted in soul when Cleon had to disgorge those five talents;Cleon had received five talents from the islanders subject to Athens, on condition that he should get the tribute payable by them reduced; when informed of this transaction, the knights compelled him to return the money. I was in ecstasy and I love the Knights for this deed; it is an honour to Greece.A hemistich borrowed from Euripides' Telephus. But the day when I was impatiently awaiting a piece by Aeschylus,The tragedies of Aeschylus continued to be played even after the poet's death, which occurred in 436 B.C., ten years before the production of The Acharnians. what tragic despair it caused me when the herald called, Theognis,A tragic poet, whose pieces were so devoid of warmth and life that he was nicknamed [the Greek for] snow. introduce your Chorus! Just imagine how this blow struck straight at my heart! On the other hand, what joy Dexitheus caused me at the musical competition, when he played a Boeotian melody on the lyre! But this year by contrast! Oh! what deadly torture to hear ChaerisA bad musician, frequently ridiculed by Aristophanes; he played both the lyre and the flute. perform the prelude in the Orthian mode!A lively and elevated method. —Never, however, since I began to bathe, has the dust hurt my eyes as it does to-day. Still it is the day of assembly; all should be here at daybreak, and yet the PnyxA hill near the Acropolis, where the Assemblies were held. is still deserted. They are gossiping in the marketplace, slipping hither and thither to avoid the vermilioned rope.Several means were used to force citizens to attend the assemblies; the shops were closed; circulation was only permitted in those streets which led to the Pnyx; finally, a rope covered with vermilion was drawn round those who dallied in the Agora (the market-place), and the late-comers, ear- marked by the imprint of the rope, were fined. The PrytanesMagistrates who, with the Archons and the Epistatae, shared the care of holding and directing the assemblies of the people; they were fifty in number. even do not come; they will be late, but when they come they will push and fight each other for a seat in the front row. They will never trouble themselves with the question of peace. Oh! Athens! Athens! As for myself, I do not fail to come here before all the rest, and now, finding myself alone, I groan, yawn, stretch, break wind, and know not what to do; I make sketches in the dust, pull out my loose hairs, muse, think of my fields, long for peace, curse town life and regret my dear country home,The Peloponnesian War had already, at the date of the representation of The Acharnians, lasted five years, 431-426 B.C.; driven from their lands by the successive Lacedaemonian invasions, the people throughout the country had been compelled to seek shelter behind the walls of Athens. which never told me to buy fuel, vinegar or oil; there the word buy, which cuts me in two, was unknown; I harvested everything at will. Therefore I have come to the assembly fully prepared to bawl, interrupt and abuse the speakers, if they talk of anything but peace. But here come the Prytanes, and high time too, for it is midday! As I foretold, hah! is it not so? They are pushing and fighting for the front seats.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Move on up, move on, move on, to get within the consecrated area.Shortly before the meeting of the Assembly, a number of young pigs were immolated and a few drops of their blood were sprinkled on the seats of the Prytanes; this sacrifice was in honour of Ceres.

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: Has anyone spoken yet?

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Who asks to speak?

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: I do.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Your name?

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: Amphitheus.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: You are no man.The name, Amphitheus, contains [the Greek] word [for] god.

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: No! I am an immortal! Amphitheus was the son of Ceres and Triptolemus; of him was born Celeus. Celeus wedded Phaenerete, my grandmother, whose son was Lucinus, and, being born of him I am an immortal; it is to me alone that the gods have entrusted the duty of treating with the Lacedaemonians. But, citizens, though I am immortal, I am dying of hunger; the Prytanes give me naught.Amongst other duties, it was the office of the Prytanes to look after the wants of the poor.

sp.speaker: A PRYTANIS
sp.p: Guards!

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: Oh, Triptolemus and Ceres, do ye thus forsake your own blood?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Prytanes, in expelling this citizen, you are offering an outrage to the Assembly. He only desired to secure peace for us and to sheathe the sword.

sp.speaker: PRYTANIS
sp.p: Sit down and keep silence!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, by Apollo, I will not, unless you are going to discuss the question of peace.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: The ambassadors, who are returned from the Court of the King!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Of what King? I am sick of all those fine birds, the peacock ambassadors and their swagger.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Silence!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh! oh! by Ecbatana,The summer residence of the Great King. what a costume!

sp.speaker: AN AMBASSADOR
sp.p: During the archonship of Euthymenes, you sent us to the Great King on a salary of two drachmae per diem.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! those poor drachmae!

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: We suffered horribly on the plains of the Cayster, sleeping under a tent, stretched deliciously on fine chariots, half dead with weariness.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And I was very much at ease, lying on the straw along the battlements!Referring to the hardships he had endured garrisoning the walls of Athens during the Lacedaemonian invasions early in the War.

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: Everywhere we were well received and forced to drink delicious wine out of golden or crystal flagons....

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, city of Cranaus,Cranaus, the second king of Athens, the successor of Cecrops. thy ambassadors are laughing at thee!

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: For great feeders and heavy drinkers are alone esteemed as men by the barbarians.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Just as here in Athens, we only esteem the most drunken debauchees.

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: At the end of the fourth year we reached the King's Court, but he had left with his whole army to ease himself, and for the space of eight months he was thus easing himself in the midst of the golden mountains.Lucian, in his Hermotimus, speaks of these golden mountains as an apocryphal land of wonders and prodigies.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And how long was he replacing his dress?

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Who ever saw an oxen baked in an oven? What a lie!

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: On my honour, he also had us served with a bird three times as large as Cleonymus,Cleonymus was an Athenian general of exceptionally tall stature; Aristophanes incessantly rallies him for his cowardice; he had cast away his buckler in a fight. and called the Boaster.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And do we give you two drachmae, that you should treat us to all this humbug?

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: We are bringing to you PseudartabasA name borne by certain officials of the King of Persia. The actor of this part wore a mask, fitted with a single eye of great size., the King's Eye.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I would a crow might pluck out thine with his beak, you cursed ambassador!

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: The King's Eye!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Eh! Great Gods! Friend, with thy great eye, round like the hole through which the oarsman passes his sweep, you have the air of a galley doubling a cape to gain port.

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: Come, Pseudartabas, give forth the message for the Athenians with which you were charged by the Great King.

sp.speaker: PSEUDARTABAS
sp.p: Jartaman exarx 'anapissonia satra.Jargon, no doubt meaningless in all languages.

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: Do you understand what he says?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: By Apollo, not I!

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR (TO THE PRYTANES)
sp.p: He says that the Great King will send you gold. Come, utter the word gold louder and more distinctly.

sp.speaker: PSEUDARTABAS
sp.p: Thou shalt not have gold, thou gaping-arsed Ionian.The Persians styled all Greeks Ionians without distinction; here the Athenians are intended.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! may the gods forgive me, but that is clear enough!

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: What does he say?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: That the Ionians are debauchees and idiots, if they expect to receive gold from the barbarians.

sp.speaker: AMBASSADOR
sp.p: Not so, he speaks of medimniA Greek measure, containing about six modii. of gold.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What medimni? Thou are but a great braggart; but get your way; I will find out the truth by myself. Come now, answer me clearly, if you do not wish me to dye your skin red. Will the Great King send us gold? (PSEUDARTABAS MAKES A NEGATIVE SIGN.) Then our ambassadors are seeking to deceive us? (PSEUDARTABAS SIGNS AFFIRMATIVELY.) These fellows make signs like any Greek; I am sure that they are nothing but Athenians. Oh! ho! I recognize one of these eunuchs; it is Clisthenes, the son of Sibyrtius.Noted for his extreme ugliness and his obscenity. Aristophanes frequently holds him to scorn in his comedies. Behold the effrontery of this shaven rump! How! great baboon, with such a beard do you seek to play the eunuch to us? And this other one? Is it not Straton? frequently holds him to scorn in his comedies.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Silence! Let all be seated. The Senate invites the King's Eye to the Prytaneum.Ambassadors were entertained there at the public expense.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Is this not sufficient to drive one to hang oneself? Here I stand chilled to the bone, whilst the doors of the Prytaneum fly wide open to lodge such rascals. But I will do something great and bold. Where is Amphitheus? Come and speak with me.

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: Here I am.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Take these eight drachmae and go and conclude a truce with the Lacedaemonians for me, my wife and my children; I leave you free, my dear citizens, to send out embassies and to stand gaping in the air.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Bring in Theorus, who has returned from the Court of Sitalces.King of Thrace.

sp.speaker: THEORUS
sp.p: I am here.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Another humbug!

sp.speaker: THEORUS
sp.p: We should not have remained long in Thrace...

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Forsooth, no, if you had not been well paid.

sp.speaker: THEORUS
sp.p: ...if the country had not been covered with snow; the rivers were ice-bound at the time that TheognisThe tragic poet. brought out his tragedy here; during the whole of that time I was holding my own with Sitalces, cup in hand; and, in truth, he adored you to such a degree, that he wrote on the walls, How beautiful are the Athenians! His son, to whom we gave the freedom of the city, burned with desire to come here and eat chitterlings at the feast of the Apaturia;A feast lasting three days and celebrated during the month Pyanepsion (November). The Greek word contains the suggestion of fraud. he prayed his father to come to the aid of his new country and Sitalces swore on his goblet that he would succour us with such a host that the Athenians would exclaim, What a cloud of grasshoppers!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: May I die if I believe a word of what you tell us! Excepting the grasshoppers, there is not a grain of truth in it all!

sp.speaker: THEORUS
sp.p: And he has sent you the most warlike soldiers of all Thrace.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Now we shall begin to see clearly.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Come hither, Thracians, whom Theorus brought.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What plague have we here?

sp.speaker: THEORUS
sp.p: 'Tis the host of the Odomanti.A Thracian tribe from the right bank of the Strymon.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Of the Odomanti? Tell me what it means. Who has mutilated them like this?

sp.speaker: THEORUS
sp.p: If they are given a wage of two drachmae, they will put all BoeotiaThe Boeotians were the allies of Sparta. to fire and sword.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Two drachmae to those circumcised hounds! Groan aloud, ye people of rowers, bulwark of Athens! Ah! great gods! I am undone; these Odomanti are robbing me of my garlic!Dicaeopolis had brought a clove of garlic with him to eat during the Assembly. Will you give me back my garlic?

sp.speaker: THEORUS
sp.p: Oh! wretched man! do not go near them; they have eaten garlicGarlic was given to game-cocks, before setting them at each other, to give them pluck for the fight..

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Prytanes, will you let me be treated in this manner, in my own country and by barbarians? But I oppose the discussion of paying a wage to the Thracians; I announce an omen; I have just felt a drop of rain.At the least unfavourable omen, the sitting of the Assembly was declared at an end.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Let the Thracians withdraw and return the day after tomorrow; the Prytanes declare the sitting at an end.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ye gods, what garlic I have lost! But here comes Amphitheus returned from Lacedaemon. Welcome, Amphitheus.

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: No, there is no welcome for me and I fly as fast as I can, for I am pursued by the Acharnians.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Why, what has happened?

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: I was hurrying to bring your treaty of truce, but some old dotards from AcharnaeThe deme of Acharnae was largely inhabited by charcoal-burners, who supplied the city with fuel. got scent of the thing; they are veterans of Marathon, tough as oak or maple, of which they are made for sure—rough and ruthless. They all started a-crying: Wretch! you are the bearer of a treaty, and the enemy has only just cut our vines! Meanwhile they were gathering stones in their cloaks, so I fled and they ran after me shouting.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Let 'em shout as much as they please! But HAVE you brought me a treaty?

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: Most certainly, here are three samples to select from,He presents them in the form of wines contained in three separate skins. this one is five years old; take it and taste.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Faugh!

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: Well?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: It does not please me; it smells of pitch and of the ships they are fitting out.Meaning, preparations for war.

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: Here is another, ten years old; taste it.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: It smells strongly of the delegates, who go around the towns to chide the allies for their slowness.Meaning, securing allies for the continuance of the war.

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: This last is a truce of thirty years, both on sea and land.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh! by Bacchus! what a bouquet! It has the aroma of nectar and ambrosia; this does not say to us, Provision yourselves for three days. But it lisps the gentle numbers, Go whither you will.When Athens sent forth an army, the soldiers were usually ordered to assemble at some particular spot with provisions for three days. I accept it, ratify it, drink it at one draught and consign the Acharnians to limbo. Freed from the war and its ills, I shall keep the DionysiaThese feasts were also called the Anthesteria or Lenaea; the Lenaem was a temple to Bacchus, erected outside the city. They took place during the month Anthesterion (February). in the country.

sp.speaker: AMPHITHEUS
sp.p: And I shall run away, for I'm mortally afraid of the Acharnians.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: This way all! Let us follow our man; we will demand him of everyone we meet; the public weal makes his seizure imperative. Ho, there! tell me which way the bearer of the truce has gone; he has escaped us, he has disappeared.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
CHORUS
sp.p: but now my limbs are stiff; old LacratidesHe had been Archon at the time of the battle of Marathon. feels his legs are weighty and the traitor escapes me. No, no, let us follow him; old Acharnians like ourselves shall not be set at naught by a scoundrel, who has dared, great gods!

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: to conclude a truce, when I wanted the war continued with double fury in order to avenge my ruined lands. No mercy for our foes until I have pierced their hearts like sharp reed, so that they dare never again ravage my vineyards.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Come, let us seek the rascal; let us look everywhere, carrying our stones in our hands; let us hunt him from place to place until we trap him; I could never, never tire of the delight of stoning him.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Peace! profane men!A sacred formula, pronounced by the priest before offering the sacrifice.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Silence all! Friends, do you hear the sacred formula? Here is he, whom we seek! This way, all! Get out of his way, surely he comes to offer an oblation.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Peace, profane men! Let the basket-bearerThe maiden who carried the basket filled with fruits at the Dionysia in honour of Bacchus. come forward, and thou Xanthias, hold the phallus well upright.The emblem of the fecundity of nature; it consisted of a representation, generally grotesquely exaggerated, of the male genital organs; the phallophori crowned with violets and ivy and their faces shaded with green foliage, sang improvised airs, call Phallics, full of obscenity and suggestive double entendres.

sp.speaker: WIFE OF DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Daughter, set down the basket and let us begin the sacrifice.

sp.speaker: DAUGHTER OF DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Mother, hand me the ladle, that I may spread the sauce on the cake.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: It is well! Oh, mighty Bacchus, it is with joy that, freed from military duty, I and all mine perform this solemn rite and offer thee this sacrifice; grant that I may keep the rural Dionysia without hindrance and that this truce of thirty years may be propitious for me.

sp.speaker: WIFE OF DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Come, my child, carry the basket gracefully and with a grave, demure face. Happy he, who shall be your possessor and embrace you so firmly at dawn,The most propitious moment for Love's gambols, observes the scholiast. that you belch wind like a weasel. Go forward, and have a care they don't snatch your jewels in the crowd.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Xanthias, walk behind the basket-bearer and hold the phallus well erect; I will follow, singing the Phallic hymn; thou, wife, look on from the top of the terrace.Married women did not join in the processions. Forward!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, Phales,The god of generation, worshipped in the form of a phallus. companion of the orgies of Bacchus, night reveller, god of adultery, friend of young men, these past sixA remark which fixes the date of the production of The Acharnians, viz. the sixth year of the Peloponnesian War, 426 B.C. years I have not been able to invoke thee. With what joy I return to my farmstead, thanks to the truce I have concluded, freed from cares, from fighting and from Lamachuses!Lamachus was an Athenian general, who figures later in this comedy. How much sweeter, oh Phales, oh, Phales, is it to surprise Thratta, the pretty woodmaid, Strymodorus' slave, stealing wood from Mount Phelleus, to catch her under the arms, to throw her on the ground and possess her, Oh, Phales, Phales! If thou wilt drink and bemuse thyself with me, we shall to-morrow consume some good dish in honour of the peace, and I will hang up my buckler over the smoking hearth.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: It is he, he himself. Stone him, stone him, stone him, strike the wretch. All, all of you, pelt him, pelt him!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What is this? By Heracles, you will smash my pot.At the rural Dionysia a pot of kitchen vegetables was borne in the procession along with other emblems.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: It is you that we are stoning, you miserable scoundrel.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And for what sin, Acharnian Elders, tell me that!

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: You ask that, you impudent rascal, traitor to your country; you alone amongst us all have concluded a truce, and you dare to look us in the face!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: But you do not know WHY I have treated for peace. Listen!

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Listen to you? No, no, you are about to die, we will annihilate you with our stones.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: But first of all, listen. Stop, my friends.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: I will hear nothing; do not address me; I hate you more than I do Cleon,Cleon the Demagogue was a currier originally by trade. He was the sworn foe and particular detestation of the Knights or aristocratic party generally. whom one day I shall flay to make sandals for the Knights.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Listen to your long speeches, after you have treated with the Laconians? No, I will punish you.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Friends, leave the Laconians out of debate and consider only whether I have not done well to conclude my truce.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Done well! when you have treated with a people who know neither gods, nor truth, nor faith.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: We attribute too much to the Laconians; as for myself, I know that they are not the cause of all our troubles.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Oh, indeed, rascal! You dare to use such language to me and then expect me to spare you!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, no, they are not the cause of all our troubles, and I who address you claim to be able to prove that they have much to complain of in us.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: This passes endurance; my heart bounds with fury. Thus you dare to defend our enemies.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Were my head on the block I would uphold what I say and rely on the approval of the people.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Comrades, let us hurl our stones and dye this fellow purple.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What black fire-brand has inflamed your heart! You will not hear me? You really will not, Acharnians?

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: No, a thousand times, no.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: This is a hateful injustice.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: May I die, if I listen.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Nay, nay! have mercy, have mercy, Acharnians.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: You shall die.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Well, blood for blood! I will kill your dearest friend. I have here the hostages of Acharnae;That is, the baskets of charcoal. I shall disembowel them.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Acharnians, what means this threat? Has he got one of our children in his house? What gives him such audacity?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Stone me, if it please you; I shall avenge myself on this. (SHOWS A BASKET.) Let us see whether you have any love for your coals.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Great Gods! this basket is our fellow-citizen. Stop, stop, in heaven's name!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I shall dismember it despite your cries; I will listen to nothing.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: How! will you kill this coal-basket, my beloved comrade?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Just now, you would not listen to me.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Well, speak now, if you will; tell us, tell us you have a weakness for the Lacedaemonians. I consent to anything; never will I forsake this dear little basket.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: First, throw down your stones.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: There! 'tis done. And you, do put away your sword.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Let me see that no stones remain concealed in your cloaks.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: They are all on the ground; see how we shake our garments. Come, no haggling, lay down your sword; we threw away everything while crossing from one side of the stage to the other.The stage of the Greek theatre was much broader, and at the same time shallower, than in a modern playhouse.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What cries of anguish you would have uttered had these coals of ParnesA mountain in Attica, in the neighbourhood of Acharnae. been dismembered, and yet it came very near it; had they perished, their death would have been due to the folly of their fellow-citizens. The poor basket was so frightened, look, it has shed a thick black dust over me, the same as a cuttle-fish does. What an irritable temper! You shout and throw stones, you will not hear my arguments—not even when I propose to speak in favour of the Lacedaemonians with my head on the block; and yet I cling to life.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Well then, bring out a block before your door, scoundrel, and let us hear the good grounds you can give us; I am curious to know them. Now mind, as you proposed yourself, place your head on the block and speak.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Here is the block; and, though I am but a very sorry speaker, I wish nevertheless to talk freely of the Lacedaemonians and without the protection of my buckler. Yet I have many reasons for fear. I know our rustics; they are delighted if some braggart comes, and rightly or wrongly, loads both them and their city with praise and flattery; they do not see that such toad-eatersOrators in the pay of the enemy. are traitors, who sell them for gain. As for the old men, I know their weakness; they only seek to overwhelm the accused with their votes.Satire on the Athenians' addiction to law-suits. Nor have I forgotten how Cleon treated me because of my comedy last year;The Babylonians. Cleon had denounced Aristophanes to the Senate for having scoffed at Athens before strangers, many of whom were present at the performance. The play is now lost. he dragged me before the Senate and there he uttered endless slanders against me; 'twas a tempest of abuse, a deluge of lies. Through what a slough of mud he dragged me! I almost perished. Permit me, therefore, before I speak, to dress in the manner most likely to draw pity.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: What evasions, subterfuges and delays! Hold! here is the sombre helmet of Pluto with its thick bristling plume; HieronymusA tragic poet; we know next to nothing of him or his works. lends it to you; then open Sisyphus'Son of Aeolus, renowned in fable for his robberies, and for the tortures to which he was put by Pluto. He was cunning enough to break loose out of hell, but Hermes brought him back again. bag of wiles; but hurry, hurry, pray, for discussion does not admit of delay.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: The time has come for me to manifest my courage, so I will go and seek Euripides. Ho! slave, slave!

sp.speaker: SLAVE
sp.p: Who's there?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Is Euripides at home?

sp.speaker: SLAVE
sp.p: He is and he isn't; understand that, if you have wit for't.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: How? He is and he isn't!This whole scene is directed at Euripides; Aristophanes ridicules the subtleties of his poetry and the trickeries of his staging, which, according to him, he only used to attract the less refined among his audience.

sp.speaker: SLAVE
sp.p: Certainly, old man; busy gathering subtle fancies here and there, his mind is not in the house, but he himself is; perched aloft, he is composing a tragedy.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, Euripides, you are indeed happy to have a slave so quick at repartee! Now, fellow, call your master.

sp.speaker: SLAVE
sp.p: Impossible!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: So much the worse. But I will not go. Come, let us knock at the door. Euripides, my little Euripides, my darling Euripides, listen; never had man greater right to your pity. It is Dicaeopolis of the Chollidan Deme who calls you. Do you hear?

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: I have no time to waste.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Very well, have yourself wheeled out here."Wheeled out"—that is, by means of a mechanical contrivance of the Greek stage, by which an interior was shown, the set scene with performers, etc., all complete, being in some way, which cannot be clearly made out from the descriptions, swung out or wheeled out on to the main stage.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Impossible.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Nevertheless...

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Well, let them roll me out; as to coming down, I have not the time.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Euripides....

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: What words strike my ear?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: You perch aloft to compose tragedies, when you might just as well do them on the ground. I am not astonished at your introducing cripples on the stage.Having been lamed, it is of course implied, by tumbling from the lofty apparatus on which the Author sat perched to write his tragedies. And why dress in these miserable tragic rags? I do not wonder that your heroes are beggars. But, Euripides, on my knees I beseech you, give me the tatters of some old piece; for I have to treat the Chorus to a long speech, and if I do it ill it is all over with me.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: What rags do you prefer? Those in which I rigged out AeneusEuripides delighted, or was supposed by his critic Aristophanes to delight, in the representation of misery and wretchedness on the stage. Aeneus, Phoenix, Philoctetes, Bellerophon, Telephus, Ino are titles of six tragedies of his in this genre of which fragments are extant. on the stage, that unhappy, miserable old man?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, I want those of some hero still more unfortunate.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Of Phoenix, the blind man?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, not of Phoenix, you have another hero more unfortunate than him.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Now, what tatters DOES he want? Do you mean those of the beggar Philoctetes?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, of another far more the mendicant.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Is it the filthy dress of the lame fellow, Bellerophon?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, 'tis not Bellerophon; he, whom I mean, was not only lame and a beggar, but boastful and a fine speaker.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Ah! I know, it is Telephus, the Mysian.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Yes, Telephus. Give me his rags, I beg of you.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Slave! give him Telephus' tatters; they are on top of the rags of Thyestes and mixed with those of Ino.

sp.speaker: SLAVE
sp.p: Catch hold! here they are.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh! Zeus, whose eye pierces everywhere and embraces all, permit me to assume the most wretched dress on earth. Euripides, cap your kindness by giving me the little Mysian hat, that goes so well with these tatters. I must to-day have the look of a beggar; be what I am, but not appear to be;Line borrowed from Euripides. A great number of verses are similarly parodied in this scene. the audience will know well who I am, but the Chorus will be fools enough not to, and I shall dupe 'em with my subtle phrases.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: I will give you the hat; I love the clever tricks of an ingenious brain like yours.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Rest happy, and may it befall Telephus as I wish. Ah! I already feel myself filled with quibbles. But I must have a beggar's staff.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Here you are, and now get you gone from this porch.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, my soul! You see how you are driven from this house, when I still need so many accessories. But let us be pressing, obstinate, importunate. Euripides, give me a little basket with a lamp alight inside.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Whatever do you want such a thing as that for?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I do not need it, but I want it all the same.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: You importune me; get you gone!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Alas! may the gods grant you a destiny as brilliant as your mother's.Report said that Euripides' mother had sold vegetables on the market.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Leave me in peace.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, just a little broken cup.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Take it and go and hang yourself. What a tiresome fellow!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! you do not know all the pain you cause me. Dear, good Euripides, nothing beyond a small pipkin stoppered with a sponge.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Miserable man! You are robbing me of an entire tragedy.Aristophanes means, of course, to imply that the whole talent of Euripides lay in these petty details of stage property. Here, take it and be off.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I am going, but, great gods! I need one thing more; unless I have it, I am a dead man. Hearken, my little Euripides, only give me this and I go, never to return. For pity's sake, do give me a few small herbs for my basket.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: You wish to ruin me then. Here, take what you want; but it is all over with my pieces!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I won't ask another thing; I'm going. I am too importunate and forget that I rouse against me the hate of kings.—Ah! wretch that I am! I am lost! I have forgotten one thing, without which all the rest is as nothing. Euripides, my excellent Euripides, my dear little Euripides, may I die if I ask you again for the smallest present; only one, the last, absolutely the last; give me some of the chervil your mother left you in her will.

sp.speaker: EURIPIDES
sp.p: Insolent hound! Slave, lock the door!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, my soul! I must go away without the chervil. Art thou sensible of the dangerous battle we are about to engage upon in defending the Lacedaemonians? Courage, my soul, we must plunge into the midst of it. Dost thou hesitate and art thou fully steeped in Euripides? That's right! do not falter, my poor heart, and let us risk our head to say what we hold for truth. Courage and boldly to the front. I wonder I am so brave.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: What do you purport doing? what are you going to say? What an impudent fellow! what a brazen heart! to dare to stake his head and uphold an opinion contrary to that of us all! And he does not tremble to face this peril. Come, it is you who desired it, speak!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Spectators, be not angered if, although I am a beggar, I dare in a Comedy to speak before the people of Athens of the public weal; Comedy too can sometimes discern what is right. I shall not please, but I shall say what is true. Besides, Cleon shall not be able to accuse me of attacking Athens before strangers;The Babylonians had been produced at a time of year when Athens was crowded with strangers; The Acharnians, on the contrary, was played in December. we are by ourselves at the festival of the Lenaea; the period when our allies send us their tribute and their soldiers is not yet. Here is only the pure wheat without chaff; as to the resident strangers settled among us, they and the citizens are one, like the straw and the ear.

I detest the Lacedaemonians with all my heart, and may Poseidon, the god of Taenarus,Sparta had been menaced with an earthquake in 427 B.C. Poseidon was The Earthshaker, god of earthquakes, as well as of the sea. cause an earthquake and overturn their dwellings! My vines also have been cut. But come (there are only friends who hear me), why accuse the Laconians of all our woes? Some men (I do not say the city, note particularly that I do not say the city), some wretches, lost in vices, bereft of honour, who were not even citizens of good stamp, but strangers, have accused the Megarians of introducing their produce fraudulently, and not a cucumber, a leveret, a suck[l]ing pig, a clove of garlic, a lump of salt was seen without its being said, Halloa! these come from Megara, and their being instantly confiscated. Thus far the evil was not serious and we were the only sufferers. But now some young drunkards go to Megara and carry off the courtesan Simaetha; the Megarians, hurt to the quick, run off in turn with two harlots of the house of Aspasia; and so for three gay women Greece is set ablaze. Then Pericles, aflame with ire on his Olympian height, let loose the lightning, caused the thunder to roll, upset Greece and passed an edict, which ran like the song, That the Megarians be banished both from our land and from our markets and from the sea and from the continent.A song by Timocreon the Rhodian, the words of which were practically identical with Pericles' decree. Meanwhile the Megarians, who were beginning to die of hunger, begged the Lacedaemonians to bring about the abolition of the decree, of which those harlots were the cause; several times we refused their demand; and from that time there was horrible clatter of arms everywhere.

You will say that Sparta was wrong, but what should she have done? Answer that. Suppose that a Lacedaemonian had seized a little SeriphianA small and insignificant island, one of the Cyclades, allied with the Athenians, like months of these islands previous to and during the first part of the Peloponnesian War. dog on any pretext and had sold it, would you have endured it quietly? Far from it, you would at once have sent three hundred vessels to sea, and what an uproar there would have been through all the city! there 'tis a band of noisy soldiery, here a brawl about the election of a Trierarch; elsewhere pay is being distributed, the Pallas figure-heads are being regilded, crowds are surging under the market porticos, encumbered with wheat that is being measured, wine-skins, oar-leathers, garlic, olives, onions in nets; everywhere are chaplets, sprats, flute-girls, black eyes; in the arsenal bolts are being noisily driven home, sweeps are being made and fitted with leathers; we hear nothing but the sound of whistles, of flutes and fifes to encourage the work-folk. That is what you assuredly would have done, and would not Telephus have done the same? So I come to my general conclusion; we have no common sense.

sp.speaker: FIRST SEMI-CHORUS
sp.p: Oh! wretch! oh! infamous man! You are naught but a beggar and yet you dare to talk to us like this! you insult their worships the informers!

sp.speaker: SECOND SEMI-CHORUS
sp.p: By Poseidon! he speaks the truth; he has not lied in a single detail.

sp.speaker: FIRST SEMI-CHORUS
sp.p: But though it be true, need he say it? But you'll have no great cause to be proud of your insolence!

sp.speaker: SECOND SEMI-CHORUS
sp.p: Where are you running to? Don't you move; if you strike this man, I shall be at you.

sp.speaker: FIRST SEMI-CHORUS
sp.p: Lamachus, whose glance flashes lightning, whose plume petrifies thy foes, help! Oh! Lamachus, my friend, the hero of my tribe and all of you, both officers and soldiers, defenders of our walls, come to my aid; else is it all over with me!

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Whence comes this cry of battle? where must I bring my aid? where must I sow dread? who wants me to uncase my dreadful Gorgon's head?A figure of Medusa's head, forming the centre of Lamachus' shield.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, Lamachus, great hero! Your plumes and your cohorts terrify me.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: This man, Lamachus, incessantly abuses Athens.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: You are but a mendicant and you dare to use language of this sort?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, brave Lamachus, forgive a beggar who speaks at hazard.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: But what have you said? Let us hear.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I know nothing about it; the sight of weapons makes me dizzy. Oh! I adjure you, take that fearful Gorgon somewhat farther away.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: There.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Now place it face downwards on the ground.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: It is done.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Give me a plume out of your helmet.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Here is a feather.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And hold my head while I vomit; the plumes have turned my stomach.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Hah! what are you proposing to do? do you want to make yourself vomit with this feather?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Is it a feather? what bird's? a braggart's?

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Ah! ah! I will rip you open.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, no, Lamachus! Violence is out of place here! But as you are so strong, why did you not circumcise me? You have all the tools you want for the operation there.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: A beggar dares thus address a general!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: How? Am I a beggar?

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: What are you then?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Who am I? A good citizen, not ambitious; a soldier, who has fought well since the outbreak of the war, whereas you are but a vile mercenary.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: They elected me...

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Yes, three cuckoos did!Indicates the character of his election, which was arranged, so Aristophanes implies, by his partisans. If I have concluded peace, 'twas disgust that drove me; for I see men with hoary heads in the ranks and young fellows of your age shirking service. Some are in Thrace getting an allowance of three drachmae, such fellows as Tisamenophoenippus and Panurgipparchides. The others are with Chares or in Chaonia, men like Geretotheodorus and Diomialazon; there are some of the same kidney, too, at Camarina and at Gela,Town in Sicily. There is a pun on the name Gela and ridiculous which it is impossible to keep in English. Apparently the Athenians had sent embassies to all parts of the Greek world to arrange treaties of alliance in view of the struggle with the Lacedaemonians; but only young debauchees of aristocratic connections had been chosen as envoys. the laughing-stock of all and sundry.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: They were elected.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And why do you always receive your pay, when none of these others ever gets any? Speak, Marilades, you have grey hair; well then, have you ever been entrusted with a mission? See! he shakes his head. Yet he is an active as well as a prudent man. And you, Dracyllus, Euphorides or Prinides, have you knowledge of Ecbatana or Chaonia? You say no, do you not? Such offices are good for the son of CaesyraA contemporary orator apparently, otherwise unknown. and Lamachus, who, but yesterday ruined with debt, never pay their shot, and whom all their friends avoid as foot passengers dodge the folks who empty their slops out of window.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Oh! in freedom's name! are such exaggerations to be borne?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Lamachus is well content; no doubt he is well paid, you know.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: But I propose always to war with the Peloponnesians, both at sea, on land and everywhere to make them tremble, and trounce them soundly.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: For my own part, I make proclamation to all Peloponnesians, Megarians and Boeotians, that to them my markets are open; but I debar Lamachus from entering them.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Convinced by this man's speech, the folk have changed their view and approve him for having concluded peace. But let us prepare for the recital of the parabasis.The parabasis in the Old Comedy was a sort of address or topical harangue addressed directly by the poet, speaking by the Chorus, to the audience. It was nearly always political in bearing, and the subject of the particular piece was for the time being set aside altogether.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Never since our poet presented Comedies, has he praised himself upon the stage; but, having been slandered by his enemies amongst the volatile Athenians, accused of scoffing at his country and of insulting the people, to-day he wishes to reply and regain for himself the inconstant Athenians. He maintains that he has done much that is good for you; if you no longer allow yourselves to be too much hoodwinked by strangers or seduced by flattery, if in politics you are no longer the ninnies you once were, it is thanks to him. Formerly, when delegates from other cities wanted to deceive you, they had but to style you, the people crowned with violets, and at the word violets you at once sat erect on the tips of your bums. Or if, to tickle your vanity, someone spoke of rich and sleek Athens, in return for that sleekness he would get all, because he spoke of you as he would have of anchovies in oil. In cautioning you against such wiles, the poet has done you great service as well as in forcing you to understand what is really the democratic principle. Thus, the strangers, who came to pay their tributes, wanted to see this great poet, who had dared to speak the truth to Athens. And so far has the fame of his boldness reached that one day the Great King, when questioning the Lacedaemonian delegates, first asked them which of the two rival cities was the superior at sea, and then immediately demanded at which it was that the comic poet directed his biting satire. Happy that city, he added, if it listens to his counsel; it will grow in power, and its victory is assured. This is why the Lacedaemonians offer you peace, if you will cede them Aegina; not that they care for the isle, but they wish to rob you of your poet.It will be remembered that Aristophanes owned land in Aegina. As for you, never lose him, who will always fight for the cause of justice in his Comedies; he promises you that his precepts will lead you to happiness, though he uses neither flattery, nor bribery, nor intrigue, nor deceit; instead of loading you with praise, he will point you to the better way.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: I scoff at Cleon's tricks and plotting; honesty and justice shall fight my cause; never will you find me a political poltroon, a prostitute to the highest bidder.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: I invoke thee, Acharnian Muse, fierce and fell as the devouring fire; sudden as the spark that bursts from the crackling oaken coal when roused by the quickening fan to fry little fishes, while others knead the dough or whip the sharp Thasian pickle with rapid hand, so break forth, my Muse, and inspire thy tribesmen with rough, vigorous, stirring strains.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: We others, now old men and heavy with years, we reproach the city; so many are the victories we have gained for the Athenian fleets that we well deserve to be cared for in our declining life; yet far from this, we are ill-used, harassed with law-suits, delivered over to the scorn of stripling orators. Our minds and bodies being ravaged with age, Poseidon should protect us, yet we have no other support than a staff. When standing before the judge, we can scarcely stammer forth the fewest words, and of justice we see but its barest shadow, whereas the accuser, desirous of conciliating the younger men, overwhelms us with his ready rhetoric; he drags us before the judge, presses us with questions, lays traps for us; the onslaught troubles, upsets and ruins poor old Tithonus, who, crushed with age, stands tongue-tied; sentenced to a fine,Everything was made the object of a law-suit in Athens. The old soldiers, inexpert at speaking, often lost the day. he weeps, he sobs and says to his friend, This fine robs me of the last trifle that was to have bought my coffin.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Is this not a scandal? What! the clepsydraA water-clock used to limit the length of speeches in the courts. is to kill the white-haired veteran, who, in fierce fighting, has so oft covered himself with glorious sweat, whose valour at Marathon saved the country! 'Twas we who pursued on the field of Marathon, whereas now 'tis wretches who pursue us to the death and crush us! What would Marpsias reply to this?A braggart speaker, fiery and pugnacious.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: What an injustice that a man, bent with age like Thucydides, should be brow-beaten by this braggart advocate, Cephisodemus,Cephisodemus was an Athenian, but through his mother possessed Scythian blood. who is as savage as the Scythian desert he was born in! Is it not to convict him from the outset? I wept tears of pity when I saw an ArcherThe city of Athens was policed by Scythian archers. maltreat this old man, who, by Ceres, when he was young and the true Thucydides, would not have permitted an insult from Ceres herself! At that date he would have floored ten orators, he would have terrified three thousand Archers with his shouts; he would have pierced the whole line of the enemy with his shafts. Ah! but if you will not leave the aged in peace, decree that the advocates be matched; thus the old man will only be confronted with a toothless greybeard, the young will fight with the braggart, the ignoble with the son of Clinias;Alcibiades. make a law that in the future, the old man can only be summoned and convicted at the courts by the aged and the young man by the youth.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: These are the confines of my market-place. All Peloponnesians, Megarians, Boeotians, have the right to come and trade here, provided they sell their wares to me and not to Lamachus. As market-inspectors I appoint these three whips of LepreanThe leather market was held in Lepros, outside the city. leather, chosen by lot. Warned away are all informers and all men of Phasis.Mean an informer ([from the Greek] to denounce). They are bringing me the pillar on which the treaty is inscribedAccording to the Athenian custom. and I shall erect it in the centre of the market, well in sight of all.

sp.speaker: A MEGARIAN
sp.p: Hail! market of Athens, beloved of Megarians. Let Zeus, the patron of friendship, witness, I regretted you as a mother mourns her son. Come, poor little daughters of an unfortunate father, try to find something to eat; listen to me with the full heed of an empty belly. Which would you prefer? To be sold or to cry with hunger?

sp.speaker: DAUGHTERS
sp.p: To be sold, to be sold!

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: That is my opinion too. But who would make so sorry a deal as to buy you? Ah! I recall me a Megarian trick; I am going to disguise you as little porkers, that I am offering for sale. Fit your hands with these hoofs and take care to appear the issue of a sow of good breed, for, if I am forced to take you back to the house, by Hermes! you will suffer cruelly of hunger! Then fix on these snouts and cram yourselves into this sack. Forget not to grunt and to say wee-wee like the little pigs that are sacrificed in the Mysteries. I must summon Dicaeopolis. Where is be? Dicaeopolis, do you want to buy some nice little porkers?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Who are you? a Megarian?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: I have come to your market.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Well, how are things at Megara?Megara was allied to Sparta and suffered during the war more than any other city because of its proximity to Athens.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: We are crying with hunger at our firesides.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: The fireside is jolly enough with a piper. But what else is doing at Megara, eh?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: What else? When I left for the market, the authorities were taking steps to let us die in the quickest manner.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: That is the best way to get you out of all your troubles.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: True.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What other news of Megara? What is wheat selling at?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: With us it is valued as highly as the very gods in heaven!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Is it salt that you are bringing?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Are you not holding back the salt?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: 'Tis garlic then?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: What! garlic! do you not at every raid grub up the ground with your pikes to pull out every single head?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What DO you bring then?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Little sows, like those they immolate at the Mysteries.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! very well, show me them.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: They are very fine; feel their weight. See! how fat and fine.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: But what is this?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: A SOW, for a certainty.Throughout this whole scene there is an obscene play upon [a] word which means in Greek both sow and a woman's organs of generation.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: You say a sow! Of what country, then?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: From Megara. What! is it not a sow then?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, I don't believe it is.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: But a sow of the human kind.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Without question, by Diocles! of my own breed! Well! What think you? will you hear them squeal?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Well, yes, I' faith, I will.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Cry quickly, wee sowlet; squeak up, hussy, or by Hermes! I take you back to the house.

sp.speaker: GIRL
sp.p: Wee-wee, wee-wee!

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Is that a little sow, or not?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Yes, it seems so; but let it grow up, and it will be a fine fat bitch.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: In five years it will be just like its mother.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: But it cannot be sacrificed.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: And why not?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: It has no tail.Sacrificial victims were bound to be perfect in every part; an animal, therefore, without a tail could not be offered.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Because it is quite young, but in good time it will have a big one, thick and red.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: The two are as like as two peas.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: They are born of the same father and mother; let them be fattened, let them grow their bristles, and they will be the finest sows you can offer to Aphrodite.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: But sows are not immolated to Aphrodite.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Not sows to Aphrodite! Why, 'tis the only goddess to whom they are offered! the flesh of my sows will be excellent on the spit.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Can they eat alone? They no longer need their mother!

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Certainly not, nor their father.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What do they like most?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Whatever is given them; but ask for yourself.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Speak! little sow.

sp.speaker: DAUGHTER
sp.p: Wee-wee, wee-wee!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Can you eat chick-pease?

sp.speaker: DAUGHTER
sp.p: Wee-wee, wee-wee, wee-wee!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And Attic figs?

sp.speaker: DAUGHTER
sp.p: Wee-wee, wee-wee!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What sharp squeaks at the name of figs. Come, let some figs be brought for these little pigs. Will they eat them? Goodness! how they munch them, what a grinding of teeth, mighty Heracles! I believe those pigs hail from the land of the Voracians. But surely 'tis impossible they have bolted all the figs!

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Yes, certainly, bar this one that I took from them.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! what funny creatures! For what sum will you sell them?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: I will give you one for a bunch of garlic, and the other, if you like, for a quart measure of salt.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I buy them of you. Wait for me here.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: The deal is done. Hermes, god of good traders, grant I may sell both my wife and my mother in the same way!

sp.speaker: AN INFORMER
sp.p: Hi! fellow, what countryman are you?

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: I am a pig-merchant from Megara.

sp.speaker: INFORMER
sp.p: I shall denounce both your pigs and yourself as public enemies.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Ah! here our troubles begin afresh!

sp.speaker: INFORMER
sp.p: Let go that sack. I will punish your Megarian lingo!The Megarians used the Doric dialect.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Dicaeopolis, Dicaeopolis, they want to denounce me.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Who dares do this thing? Inspectors, drive out the informers. Ah! you offer to enlighten us without a lamp!A play upon [a] word which both means to light and to denounce.

sp.speaker: INFORMER
sp.p: What! I may not denounce our enemies?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Have a care for yourself, if you don't go off pretty quick to denounce elsewhere.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: What a plague to Athens!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Be reassured, Megarian. Here is the price for your two swine, the garlic and the salt. Farewell and much happiness!

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Ah! we never have that amongst us.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Well! may the inopportune wish apply to myself.

sp.speaker: MEGARIAN
sp.p: Farewell, dear little sows, and seek, far from your father, to munch your bread with salt, if they give you any.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Here is a man truly happy. See how everything succeeds to his wish. Peacefully seated in his market, he will earn his living; woe to Ctesias,An informer (sycophant), otherwise unknown. and all other informers who dare to enter there!

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: You will not be cheated as to the value of wares, you will not again see PrepisA debauchee of vile habits; a pathic. wiping his foul rump, nor will CleonymusMentioned above; he was as proud as he was cowardly. jostle you; you will take your walks, clothed in a fine tunic, without meeting HyperbolusAn Athenian general, quarrelsome and litigious, and an Informer into the bargain. and his unceasing quibblings,

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: without being accosted on the public place by any importunate fellow, neither by Cratinus,A comic poet of vile habits. shaven in the fashion of the debauchees, nor by this musician, who plagues us with his silly improvisations, Artemo, with his arm-pits stinking as foul as a goat, like his father before him.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: You will not be the butt of the villainous Pauson'sA painter. jeers, nor of Lysistratus,A debauchee, a gambler, and always in extreme poverty. the disgrace of the Cholargian deme, who is the incarnation of all the vices, and endures cold and hunger more than thirty days in the month.

sp.speaker: A BOEOTIAN
sp.p: By Heracles! my shoulder is quite black and blue. Ismenias, put the penny-royal down there very gently, and all of you, musicians from Thebes, pipe with your bone flutes into a dog's rump.This kind of flute had a bellows, made of dog-skin, much like the bagpipes of to-day.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Enough, enough, get you gone. Rascally hornets, away with you! Whence has sprung this accursed swarm of CharisA flute-player, mentioned above. fellows which comes assailing my door?

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: Ah! by Iolas!A hero, much honored in Thebes; nephew of Heracles. Drive them off, my dear host, you will please me immensely; all the way from Thebes, they were there piping behind me and have completely stripped my penny-royal of its blossom. But will you buy anything of me, some chickens or some locusts?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! good day, Boeotian, eater of good round loaves.A form of bread peculiar to Boeotia. What do you bring?

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: All that is good in Boeotia, marjoram, penny-royal, rush-mats, lamp-wicks, ducks, jays, woodcocks, water-fowl, wrens, divers.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: 'Tis a very hail of birds that beats down on my market.

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: I also bring geese, hares, foxes, moles, hedgehogs, cats, lyres, martins, otters and eels from the Copaic lake.A lake in Boeotia.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! my friend, you, who bring me the most delicious of fish, let me salute your eels.

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: Come, thou, the eldest of my fifty Copaic virgins, come and complete the joy of our host.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh! my well-beloved, thou object of my long regrets, thou art here at last then, thou, after whom the comic poets sigh, thou, who art dear to Morychus.He was the Lucullus of Athens. Slaves, hither with the stove and the bellows. Look at this charming eel, that returns to us after six long years of absence.This again fixes the date of the presentation of The Acharnians to 436 B.C., the sixth year of the War, since the beginning of which Boeotia had been closed to the Athenians. Salute it, my children; as for myself, I will supply coal to do honour to the stranger. Take it into my house; death itself could not separate me from her, if cooked with beet leaves. fA comic poet of vile habits. He was the Lucullus of Athens. fA painter. This again fixes the date of the presentation of The Acharnians to 436 B.C., the sixth year of the War, since the beginning of which Boeotia had been closed to the Athenians.

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: And what will you give me in return?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: It will pay for your market dues. And as to the rest, what do you wish to sell me?

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: Why, everything.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: On what terms? For ready-money or in wares from these parts?

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: I would take some Athenian produce, that we have not got in Boeotia.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Phaleric anchovies, pottery?

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: Anchovies, pottery? But these we have. I want produce that is wanting with us and that is plentiful here.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! I have the very thing; take away an Informer, packed up carefully as crockery-ware.

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: By the twin gods! I should earn big money, if I took one; I would exhibit him as an ape full of spite.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Hah! here we have Nicarchus,An informer. who comes to denounce you. fThis kind of flute had a bellows, made of dog-skin, much like the bagpipes of to-day. An informer.

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: How small he is!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: But in his case the whole is one mass of ill-nature.

sp.speaker: NICARCHUS
sp.p: Whose are these goods?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Mine; they come from Boeotia, I call Zeus to witness.

sp.speaker: NICARCHUS
sp.p: I denounce them as coming from an enemy's country.

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: What! you declare war against birds?

sp.speaker: NICARCHUS
sp.p: And I am going to denounce you too.

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: What harm have I done you?

sp.speaker: NICARCHUS
sp.p: I will say it for the benefit of those that listen; you introduce lamp-wicks from an enemy's country.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Then you go as far as denouncing a wick.

sp.speaker: NICARCHUS
sp.p: It needs but one to set an arsenal afire.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: A wick set an arsenal ablaze! But how, great gods?

sp.speaker: NICARCHUS
sp.p: Should a Boeotian attach it to an insect's wing, and, taking advantage of a violent north wind, throw it by means of a tube into the arsenal and the fire once get hold of the vessels, everything would soon be devoured by the flames.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! wretch! an insect and a wick devour everything! (HE STRIKES HIM.)

sp.speaker: NICARCHUS
sp.p: You will bear witness, that he mishandles me.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Shut his mouth. Give me some hay; I am going to pack him up like a vase, that he may not get broken on the road.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Pack up your goods carefully, friend; that the stranger may not break it when taking it away.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I shall take great care with it, for one would say he is cracked already; he rings with a false note, which the gods abhor.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: But what will be done with him?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: This is a vase good for all purposes; it will be used as a vessel for holding all foul things, a mortar for pounding together law-suits, a lamp for spying upon accounts, and as a cup for the mixing up and poisoning of everything.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: None could ever trust a vessel for domestic use that has such a ring about it.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh! it is strong, my friend, and will never get broken, if care is taken to hang it head downwards.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: There! it is well packed now!

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: Marry, I will proceed to carry off my bundle.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Farewell, worthiest of strangers, take this informer, good for anything, and fling him where you like.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Bah! this rogue has given me enough trouble to pack! Here! Boeotian, pick up your pottery.

sp.speaker: BOEOTIAN
sp.p: Stoop, Ismenias, that I may put it on your shoulder, and be very careful with it.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: You carry nothing worth having; however, take it, for you will profit by your bargain; the Informers will bring you luck.

sp.speaker: A SERVANT OF LAMACHUS
sp.p: Dicaeopolis!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What do you want crying this gait?

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: Lamachus wants to keep the Feast of Cups,The second day of the Dionysia or feasts of Bacchus, kept in the month Anthesterion (February), and called the Anthesteria. They lasted three days; the second being the Feast of Cups, the third the Feast of Pans. Vases, filled with grain of all kinds, were borne in procession and dedicated to Hermes. and I come by his order to bid you one drachma for some thrushes and three more for a Copaic eel.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And who is this Lamachus, who demands an eel?

sp.speaker: SERVANT
sp.p: 'Tis the terrible, indefatigable Lamachus, who is always brandishing his fearful Gorgon's head and the three plumes which o'ershadow his helmet.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, no, he will get nothing, even though he gave me his buckler. Let him eat salt fish, while he shakes his plumes, and, if he comes here making any din, I shall call the inspectors. As for myself, I shall take away all these goods; I go home on thrushes' wings and black-birds' pinions.A parody on some verses from a lost poet.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: You see, citizens, you see the good fortune which this man owes to his prudence, to his profound wisdom. You see how, since he has concluded peace, he buys what is useful in the household and good to eat hot. All good things flow towards him unsought. Never will I welcome the god of war in my house; never shall he chant the Harmodius at my table;A feasting song in honor of Harmodius, the assassin of Hipparchus the Tyrant, son of Pisistratus. he is a sot, who comes feasting with those who are overflowing with good things and brings all manner of mischief at his heels. He overthrows, ruins, rips open; 'tis vain to make him a thousand offers, be seated, pray, drink this cup, proffered in all friendship, he burns our vine-stocks and brutally pours out the wine from our vineyards on the ground. This man, on the other hand, covers his table with a thousand dishes; proud of his good fortunes, he has had these feathers cast before his door to show us how he lives.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh, Peace! companion of fair Aphrodite and of the sweet Graces, how charming are thy features and yet I never knew it! Would that Eros might join me to thee, Eros, crowned with roses as ZeuxisThe celebrated painter, born in Heraclea, a contemporary of Aristophanes. shows him to us! Perhaps I seem somewhat old to you, but I am yet able to make you a threefold offering; despite my age I could plant a long row of vines for you; then beside these some tender cuttings from the fig; finally a young vine-stock, loaded with fruit and all around the field olive trees, which would furnish us with oil, wherewith to anoint us both at the New Moons.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: List, ye people! As was the custom of your forebears, empty a full pitcher of wine at the call of the trumpet; he, who first sees the bottom, shall get a wine-skin as round and plump as Ctesiphon's belly.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Women, children, have you not heard? Faith! do you not heed the herald? Quick! let the hares boil and roast merrily; keep them a-turning; withdraw them from the flame; prepare the chaplets; reach me the skewers that I may spit the thrushes.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: I envy you your wisdom and even more your good cheer.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What then will you say when you see the thrushes roasting?

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: Ah! true indeed!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Slave! stir up the fire.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: See, how he knows his business, what a perfect cook! How well he understands the way to prepare a good dinner!

sp.speaker: A HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: Ah! woe is me!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Heracles! What have we here?

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: A most miserable man.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Keep your misery for yourself.

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: Ah! friend! since you alone are enjoying peace, grant me a part of your truce, were it but five years.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What has happened to you?

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: I am ruined; I have lost a pair of steers.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: The Boeotians seized them at Phyle.A deme and frontier fortress of Attica, near the Boeotian border.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! poor wretch! and yet you have not left off white?

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: Their dung made my wealth.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What can I do in the matter?

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: Crying for my beasts has lost me my eyesight. Ah! if you care for poor Dercetes of Phyle, anoint mine eyes quickly with your balm of peace.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: But, my poor fellow, I do not practise medicine.

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: Come, I adjure you; perhaps I shall recover my steers.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: 'Tis impossible; away, go and whine to the disciples of Pittalus.An Athenian physician of the day.

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: Grant me but one drop of peace; pour it into this reedlet.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: No, not a particle; go a-weeping elsewhere.

sp.speaker: HUSBANDMAN
sp.p: Oh! oh! oh! my poor beasts!

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: This man has discovered the sweetest enjoyment in peace; he will share it with none.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Pour honey over this tripe; set it before the fire to dry.

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: What lofty tones he uses! Did you hear him?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Get the eels on the gridiron!

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: You are killing me with hunger; your smoke is choking your neighbours, and you split our ears with your bawling.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Have this fried and let it be nicely browned.

sp.speaker: A BRIDESMAID
sp.p: Dicaeopolis! Dicaeopolis!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Who are you?

sp.speaker: BRIDESMAID
sp.p: A young bridegroom sends you these viands from the marriage feast.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Whoever he be, I thank him.

sp.speaker: BRIDESMAID
sp.p: And in return, he prays you to pour a glass of peace into this vase, that he may not have to go to the front and may stay at home to do his duty to his young wife.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Take back, take back your viands; for a thousand drachmae I would not give a drop of peace; but who are you, pray?

sp.speaker: BRIDESMAID
sp.p: I am the bridesmaid; she wants to say something to you from the bride privately.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Come, what do you wish to say? (THE BRIDESMAID WHISPERS IN HIS EAR.) Ah! what a ridiculous demand! The bride burns with longing to keep by her her husband's weapon. Come! \bring hither my truce; to her alone will I give some of it, for she is a woman, and, as such, should not suffer under the war. Here, friend, reach hither your vial. And as to the manner of applying this balm, tell the bride, when a levy of soldiers is made to rub some in bed on her husband, where most needed. There, slave, take away my truce! Now, quick, bring me the wine-flagon, that I may fill up the drinking bowls!

sp.speaker: CHORUS
sp.p: I see a man, striding along apace, with knitted brows; he seems to us the bearer of terrible tidings.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Oh! toils and battles, 'tis Lamachus!

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: What noise resounds around my dwelling, where shines the glint of arms.

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: The Generals order you forthwith to take your battalions and your plumes, and, despite the snow, to go and guard our borders. They have learnt that a band of Boeotians intend taking advantage of the Feast of Cups to invade our country.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Ah! the Generals! they are numerous, but not good for much! It's cruel, not to be able to enjoy the feast!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Oh! warlike host of Lamachus!

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Wretch! do you dare to jeer me?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Do you want to fight this four-winged Geryon?

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Oh! oh! what fearful tidings!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Ah! ah! I see another herald running up; what news does he bring me?

sp.speaker: HERALD
sp.p: Dicaeopolis!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What is the matter?

sp.speaker: HERALD
LAMACHUS
sp.p: Oh! hostile gods!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: This is not astounding; you have chosen this huge, great ugly Gorgon's head for your patron. You, shut the door, and let someone get ready the meal.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Slave! slave! my knapsack!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Slave! slave! a basket!

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Take salt and thyme, slave, and don't forget the onions.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Get some fish for me; I cannot bear onions.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Slave, wrap me up a little stale salt meat in a fig-leaf.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And for me some good greasy tripe in a fig-leaf; I will have it cooked here.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Bring me the plumes for my helmet.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Bring me wild pigeons and thrushes.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: How white and beautiful are these ostrich feathers!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: How fat and well browned is the flesh of this wood-pigeon!

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Bring me the case for my triple plume.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Pass me over that dish of hare.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: OH! the moths have eaten the hair of my crest.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I shall always eat hare before dinner.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Hi! friend! try not to scoff at my armor?

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Hi! friend! will you kindly not stare at my thrushes.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Hi! friend! will you kindly not address me.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: I do not address you; I am scolding my slave. Shall we wager and submit the matter to Lamachus, which of the two is the best to eat, a locust or a thrush?

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Insolent hound!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: He much prefers the locusts.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Slave, unhook my spear and bring it to me.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Slave, slave, take the sausage from the fire and bring it to me.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Come, let me draw my spear from its sheath. Hold it, slave, hold it tight.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And you, slave, grip, grip well hold of the skewer.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Slave, the bracings for my shield.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Pull the loaves out of the oven and bring me these bracings of my stomach.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: My round buckler with the Gorgon's head.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: My round cheese-cake.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: What clumsy wit!

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: What delicious cheese-cake!

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Pour oil on the buckler. Hah! hah! I can see reflected there an old man who will be accused of cowardice.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Pour honey on the cake. Hah! hah! I can see an old man who makes Lamachus of the Gorgon's head weep with rage.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Slave, full war armour.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Slave, my beaker; that is MY armour.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: With this I hold my ground with any foe.

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: And I with this with any tosspot.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
sp.p: Fasten the strappings to the buckler; personally I shall carry the knapsack

sp.speaker: DICAEOPOLIS
sp.p: Pack the dinner well into the basket; personally I shall carry the cloak.

sp.speaker: LAMACHUS
